expectedText:
APPOINTMENT OF MINOR'S COUNSEL IN CUSTODY PROCEEDINGS — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Riley Lee · Jordan Alex Lee

CASE AND APPOINTMENT RECORD
This information sheet concerns the appointment of counsel to represent Riley Lee under California Family Code § 3150 et seq. in the custody or visitation proceeding captioned Superior Court of California, County of Sacramento, Case No. CGC-26-123456, filed in Sacramento County, involving Jordan Alex Lee and Morgan Casey Lee as parties. [If counsel has been appointed for Riley Lee in this proceeding, the appointed counsel's name may be recorded here: Jordan T. Reyes, Esq.] This document states facts about California's statutory scheme for appointment of minor's counsel. It is not itself an application, motion, or order, and it does not appoint counsel for Riley Lee or determine who pays for that counsel — only a court order can do that.

WHEN A COURT MAY APPOINT MINOR'S COUNSEL, AND HOW THE APPOINTMENT CONTINUES
Under California Family Code § 3150(a), if the court determines that it would be in Riley Lee's best interest, the court may appoint private counsel to represent Riley Lee's interests in a custody or visitation proceeding, provided that the court and counsel comply with the requirements set forth in Rules 5.240, 5.241, and 5.242 of the California Rules of Court. The statute states this appointment in discretionary terms — the court "may appoint" counsel — tied to the court's own determination of Riley Lee's best interest, rather than a right either parent can invoke or a showing that triggers a mandatory appointment. Once counsel has entered an appearance for Riley Lee under this chapter, Family Code § 3150(b) provides that counsel continues to represent Riley Lee unless relieved by the court upon the substitution of other counsel or for cause.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "If the court determines that it would be in the best interest of the minor child, the court may appoint private counsel to represent the interests of the child in a custody or visitation proceeding, provided that the court and counsel comply with the requirements set forth in Rules 5.240, 5.241, and 5.242 of the California Rules of Court."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3150(a) (California Legislative Information text), Fam. Code § 3150(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3150.)
  "Upon entering an appearance on behalf of a child pursuant to this chapter, counsel shall continue to represent that child unless relieved by the court upon the substitution of other counsel by the court or for cause."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3150(b) (California Legislative Information text), Fam. Code § 3150(b) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3150.)
  Known gap: Family Code § 3150 states only a discretionary standard — this document found no provision in §§ 3150-3153 making appointment of minor's counsel mandatory in any circumstance; the research brief for this document assumed the statute might state both permissive and mandatory grounds, and that assumption does not match the actual current text. Section 3150(a) also does not define "best interest" for this purpose, and it cross-references California Rules of Court 5.240, 5.241, and 5.242 for procedural requirements that this document does not independently verify or summarize. Section 3150(b) does not define "cause" for relieving counsel, leaving that determination to the court.

HOW MINOR'S COUNSEL DIFFERS FROM A GUARDIAN AD LITEM
California law recognizes two distinct court appointments concerning a child or minor in litigation, and this document covers only one of them. A guardian ad litem, appointed under Code of Civil Procedure § 372 (covered in this corpus's separate Guardian Ad Litem Appointment document), exists because a minor or a person who lacks legal capacity generally cannot appear as a party in a civil action or proceeding at all without one; that appointee's litigation authority is tied to court approval of specific case decisions such as compromising the action. Minor's counsel, appointed under Family Code § 3150 specifically in a custody or visitation proceeding, is a separate appointment that does not depend on Riley Lee being otherwise unable to appear as a party — Riley Lee is ordinarily not a party to the custody proceeding at all. Family Code § 3151(a) charges minor's counsel with "the representation of the child's best interests" and directs that, if Riley Lee so desires, counsel must present Riley Lee's wishes to the court — combining independent best-interest advocacy with a duty to report the child's own stated preferences, which is a different function from a guardian ad litem's role of enabling a minor to appear in litigation at all.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "The child’s counsel appointed under this chapter is charged with the representation of the child’s best interests."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3151(a) (California Legislative Information text), Fam. Code § 3151(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3151.)
  "If the child so desires, the child’s counsel shall present the child’s wishes to the court."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3151(a) (California Legislative Information text), Fam. Code § 3151(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3151.)
  Known gap: This clause's description of the guardian ad litem role rests on Code of Civil Procedure § 372 text already verified elsewhere in this corpus's separate guardian ad litem document; that statute was not independently refetched or re-quoted in this session, so this clause cites only Family Code § 3151(a) directly. Family Code §§ 3150-3153 do not themselves state whether the same child could simultaneously have both a guardian ad litem and minor's counsel in overlapping or related proceedings, and this document does not resolve that question.

SCOPE OF MINOR'S COUNSEL'S DUTIES TOWARD THE CHILD
Family Code § 3151(a) describes minor's counsel's role as gathering evidence bearing on Riley Lee's best interests and presenting that admissible evidence to the court in any manner appropriate for counsel of a party. Unless it is inappropriate under the circumstances to exercise a given duty, § 3151(a) lists counsel's duties as including interviewing Riley Lee, reviewing the court files and all accessible relevant records available to both parties, and making any further investigations counsel considers necessary to ascertain evidence relevant to the custody or visitation hearings.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "The role of the child’s counsel is to gather evidence that bears on the best interests of the child, and present that admissible evidence to the court in any manner appropriate for the counsel of a party."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3151(a) (California Legislative Information text), Fam. Code § 3151(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3151.)
  "The counsel’s duties, unless under the circumstances it is inappropriate to exercise the duty, include interviewing the child, reviewing the court files and all accessible relevant records available to both parties, and making any further investigations as the counsel considers necessary to ascertain evidence relevant to the custody or visitation hearings."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3151(a) (California Legislative Information text), Fam. Code § 3151(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3151.)
  Known gap: Family Code § 3151(a) does not define what circumstances make exercising a listed duty "inappropriate," leaving that judgment to counsel and the court. The statute requires counsel to present the child's wishes if the child so desires, but does not state how counsel is to reconcile a best-interest recommendation that differs from the child's stated wishes; this document does not resolve that question beyond quoting what § 3151(a) itself says.

MINOR'S COUNSEL'S PROCEDURAL POWERS AND ACCESS TO THE CHILD AND RECORDS
Family Code § 3151(b) requires counsel to serve notices and pleadings on all parties consistent with the requirements for parties, and provides that counsel shall not be called as a witness in the proceeding; counsel may introduce and examine counsel's own witnesses, present arguments to the court concerning Riley Lee's welfare, and participate further in the proceeding to the degree necessary to represent Riley Lee adequately. Family Code § 3151(c) lists eight specific rights held by minor's counsel, including reasonable access to Riley Lee, standing to seek affirmative relief on Riley Lee's behalf, and notice of any proceeding or phase of a proceeding affecting Riley Lee. Among those listed rights, § 3151(c)(5) gives counsel access to Riley Lee's medical, dental, mental health, and other health care records and educational records, and the right to interview school personnel, caretakers, health care providers, and mental health professionals who have assessed or cared for Riley Lee — release of that information to counsel does not itself waive the confidentiality of those records.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "Counsel shall serve notices and pleadings on all parties, consistent with requirements for parties. Counsel shall not be called as a witness in the proceeding. Counsel may introduce and examine counsel’s own witnesses, present arguments to the court concerning the child’s welfare, and participate further in the proceeding to the degree necessary to represent the child adequately."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3151(b) (California Legislative Information text), Fam. Code § 3151(b) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3151.)
  "The child’s counsel shall have the following rights: (1) Reasonable access to the child. (2) Standing to seek affirmative relief on behalf of the child. (3) Notice of any proceeding, and all phases of that proceeding, including a request for examination affecting the child."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3151(c) (California Legislative Information text), Fam. Code § 3151(c) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3151.)
  "Access to the child’s medical, dental, mental health, and other health care records, school and educational records, and the right to interview school personnel, caretakers, health care providers, mental health professionals, and others who have assessed the child or provided care to the child. The release of this information to counsel shall not constitute a waiver of the confidentiality of the reports, files, and any disclosed communications."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3151(c)(5) (California Legislative Information text), Fam. Code § 3151(c)(5) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3151.)
  Known gap: This clause quotes § 3151(b) and a representative subset of the eight enumerated rights in § 3151(c) — reasonable access, standing, notice, and records access — rather than every numbered right; § 3151(c) also separately addresses counsel's right to take any action available to a party, to receive advance notice of and refuse a non-court-ordered examination, to assert or waive privilege on the child's behalf, and to seek an independent evaluation with court approval, which this document does not quote in full here. Section 3151(c)(5) also cross-references Family Code §§ 3177 and 3182 governing counsel's interviews of mediators; those cross-referenced sections were not independently fetched or verified in this session.

MINOR'S COUNSEL'S ACCESS TO CHILD PROTECTIVE SERVICES RECORDS
Family Code § 3152(a) lets minor's counsel, upon noticed motion to all parties and the local child protective services agency, request the court to authorize release of relevant reports or files concerning Riley Lee held by the relevant local child protective services agency. Under § 3152(b), the court reviews those reports or files in camera to determine whether they are relevant to the pending action and whether, and to what extent, they should be released to counsel. Section 3152(c) provides that neither the court's in camera review nor release to counsel waives the confidentiality of the reports or files, and that counsel may not disclose their contents or existence to anyone unless otherwise permitted by law.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "The child’s counsel may, upon noticed motion to all parties and the local child protective services agency, request the court to authorize release of relevant reports or files, concerning the child represented by the counsel, of the relevant local child protective services agency."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3152(a) (California Legislative Information text), Fam. Code § 3152(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3152.)
  "The court shall review the reports or files in camera in order to determine whether they are relevant to the pending action and whether and to what extent they should be released to the child’s counsel."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3152(b) (California Legislative Information text), Fam. Code § 3152(b) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3152.)
  "Neither the review by the court nor the release to counsel shall constitute a waiver of the confidentiality of the reports and files. Counsel shall not disclose the contents or existence of the reports or files to anyone unless otherwise permitted by law."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3152(c) (California Legislative Information text), Fam. Code § 3152(c) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3152.)
  Known gap: Family Code § 3152 does not define "relevant" for purposes of the court's in camera determination, does not set a deadline for the noticed motion, and does not state what "otherwise permitted by law" means for purposes of counsel's nondisclosure duty in § 3152(c); this document does not resolve those undefined terms.

COMPENSATION FOR MINOR'S COUNSEL AND ALLOCATION OF THE COST
Family Code § 3153(a) provides that, if the court appoints counsel under this chapter to represent Riley Lee, counsel receives a reasonable sum for compensation and expenses in an amount the court determines, and — except as provided in subdivision (b) — that amount is paid by the parties in the proportions the court deems just. Section 3153(b) adds a county-pay fallback: on its own motion or a party's motion, the court determines whether Jordan Alex Lee and Morgan Casey Lee together are financially unable to pay all or part of the cost of appointed counsel, and whatever portion the court finds the parties unable to pay is paid by the county; the Judicial Council adopts guidelines to assist in determining financial eligibility for that county payment.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "If the court appoints counsel under this chapter to represent the child, counsel shall receive a reasonable sum for compensation and expenses, the amount of which shall be determined by the court. Except as provided in subdivision (b), this amount shall be paid by the parties in the proportions the court deems just."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3153(a) (California Legislative Information text), Fam. Code § 3153(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3153.)
  "Upon its own motion or that of a party, the court shall determine whether both parties together are financially unable to pay all or a portion of the cost of counsel appointed pursuant to this chapter, and the portion of the cost of that counsel which the court finds the parties are unable to pay shall be paid by the county. The Judicial Council shall adopt guidelines to assist in determining financial eligibility for county payment of counsel appointed by the court pursuant to this chapter."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3153(b) (California Legislative Information text), Fam. Code § 3153(b) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3153.)
  Known gap: The research brief's framing of this section as allocating cost only "between the parties" does not match the actual text — § 3153(b) makes a county-pay fallback part of the statutory scheme whenever the court finds the parties financially unable to pay all or part of the cost, not merely a discretionary option. Section 3153 does not itself state how a "reasonable sum" for compensation is calculated (for example, by hourly rate or flat fee) or what the Judicial Council's financial-eligibility guidelines require; this document does not independently source or summarize those guidelines.

RECORD AND SIGNATURE BLOCK
Prepared/reviewed on September 1, 2026 at Oakland, California.
